title: [Dropbox Tech] Improving infrastructure efficiency for growing demand in the age of AI
summary: As demand for AI continues to grow, so does the infrastructure needed to support it. Much of the industry's attention has focused on building more: more data centers, more servers, and more power. But building new infrastructure is only part of the challenge. Engineering teams are also working within constraints on energy, cooling, hardware availability, and physical space, making it increasingly important to get more from the infrastructure that's already in place. For over a decade, Dropbox’s Infrastructure and Datacenter Engineering teams have continually improved how we plan, operate, and optimize infrastructure. That work spans far more than storage systems. Engineers across Dropbox work together on capacity planning, fleet optimization, hardware lifecycle management, power delivery, cooling, rack design, and facility planning. Rather than treating these as independent problems, we optimize them as parts of a single system, where decisions in one layer influence what's possible in another. The result is an engineering discipline that extends beyond any single system or optimization. A change in one part of the infrastructure can create opportunities or constraints elsewhere. Increasing storage density, for example, can reduce the amount of hardware needed, while more powerful servers can introduce new energy and cooling requirements. Understanding those tradeoffs allows us to make infrastructure decisions with the entire system in mind. As infrastructure demand grows, that system-level approach helps us prioritize efficiency and create room for growth before expanding our data center footprint. Planning for efficient infrastructure Many of the decisions that shape infrastructure efficiency happen months or sometimes years before new capacity goes into production. Whether someone is uploading a file to Dropbox or asking Dash a question, they expect the product to respond without delay. Delivering that experience requires engineers to forecast how customer demand and workloads will change, determine when additional resources will be needed, and understand whether our existing environments can support them. Dropbox has operated large-scale infrastructure for over a decade. Our hybrid model combines Magic Pocket, the core Dropbox storage system, with colocated data centers, where we manage our own servers and networking equipment in facilities operated by specialized providers. This gives our engineers visibility across software, hardware, and the physical data center environment. As customer demand grows and workloads change, particularly with the growth of AI-powered products and features, engineers have to plan not only for how much additional capacity is needed, but where and how it can be deployed. New hardware has to fit within a facility's infrastructure constraints while accounting for hardware availability and future product needs. A server that provides more compute or storage, for example, may also require more energy or cooling, changing how much hardware a rack or facility can support. The goal is to understand those tradeoffs early, add capacity deliberately, and preserve enough headroom for growth, maintenance, failures, and changing workloads. Once additional compute and storage capacity is deployed, the focus shifts to making the most of the systems already in production. Continuously optimizing the active fleet Planning helps ensure infrastructure is ready for anticipated demand, but workloads rarely behave exactly as they did when that infrastructure was first deployed. Customer behavior changes, products evolve, and new capabilities introduce different demands on the underlying systems. AI is a prime example because AI-powered features can change both the scale and shape of infrastructure demand, placing new demands on compute, storage, memory, and networking. That makes efficiency an ongoing engineering problem. Rather than treating deployed infrastructure as fixed, Dropbox continually adapts how the active fleet operates as those demands change. Sometimes that means reducing how much hardware is in use when demand is lower. Sometimes it means shifting work to parts of the fleet with resources available. And in other instances, advances in hardware allow the same physical infrastructure to support substantially more storage. These approaches work at different layers of the system, but they share the same objective: getting more useful capacity from the infrastructure already in place before adding more of it. Letting capacity rest when it isn't needed Infrastructure has to be provisioned for periods of higher demand, with additional headroom built in for reliability and maintenance. That means not all available capacity is needed at all times. When hardware is sitting idle or excess capacity is available, keeping every component fully powered consumes energy without providing additional value. Deep Sleep is one way Dropbox reduces that overhead. Deep Sleep is a Dropbox infrastructure initiative that reduces power consumption when hardware isn't actively needed. Depending on the hardware, that can mean spinning down hard drives into standby mode or powering down idle servers altogether. A server becomes eligible for Deep Sleep through automated fleet management algorithms. Dropbox is able to balance energy efficiency with performance and reliability because servers can return to service within minutes. For workloads that require lower latency, we can also selectively spin down idle hard drives rather than powering down the entire server. The challenge is determining where those power-saving measures can be applied safely. Engineers have to preserve enough available capacity to meet operational and reliability requirements while identifying hardware that doesn't need to remain fully powered. That allows Dropbox to reduce the energy consumed by underused infrastructure without compromising the capacity our products depend on. Reducing the power consumed by idle hardware is one way to make the existing fleet more efficient. Another is making better use of the infrastructure that's already online. Balancing work across the fleet Having enough capacity to meet overall demand is only part of operating infrastructure efficiently. That capacity also needs to be available where the work is happening. One part of the fleet may be approaching its limits while another has room to take on more work. Without a way to address that imbalance, Dropbox could end up adding more infrastructure instead of making better use of what’s already available across the fleet. To avoid that, Dropbox continually monitors how workloads are using resources across our infrastructure. The team identifies imbalances by monitoring spare capacity and workload distribution across the fleet, looking for areas where available headroom is falling or work is concentrating unevenly. When demand is uneven, teams can rebalance workloads across systems or bring additional capacity online where it's needed. Some adjustments happen automatically, while larger changes are reviewed and validated by engineers. This allows us to take advantage of available resources elsewhere rather than treating a localized constraint as a need for more infrastructure overall. That balancing has to continue as the fleet changes. Customer behavior shifts, products introduce new workload patterns, and the infrastructure itself evolves. Continually adapting where work runs helps Dropbox get more from the capacity that's already online. Balancing workloads helps make better use of the capacity we already have, but efficiency can also come from increasing how much that infrastructure can support in the first place. Increasing storage density Another way to get more from existing infrastructure is to increase how much each piece of hardware can support. Advances in storage technology have allowed Dropbox to store significantly more customer data on each drive. One example is shingled magnetic recording, which packs data more densely onto a hard drive without increasing its physical size. Those gains compound across the infrastructure. When each drive holds more data, fewer drives are needed to provide the same amount of storage. That can mean fewer servers and racks, less cabling, and lower power and cooling requirements. In turn, increasing the capacity of a single component can reduce the resources required across an entire deployment. That system-level impact is also why total power consumption doesn't tell the full story of efficiency. As Dropbox grows and stores more customer data, overall energy use may increase even as the infrastructure becomes more efficient. A more useful measure is watts per petabyte, or the amount of power required to support a petabyte of storage. Since 2020, watts per petabyte across our storage infrastructure have improved by more than 50%. Today, it takes less than half as much power to support the same amount of storage as it did in 2020. Together, all of the approaches described above help Dropbox get more from existing infrastructure by reducing unnecessary power consumption, making better use of available capacity and increasing how much each piece of hardware can support. How long that hardware can reliably remain in service matters, too. Extending infrastructure over time Replacing equipment too early can leave useful capacity on the table, while keeping it too long can introduce reliability and performance risks. Hardware doesn’t become unreliable simply because it reaches a particular age, nor does keeping equipment longer always make sense. To make those decisions, Dropbox monitors how hardware performs in production. Metrics such as annual failure rate help engineers understand how different components and generations of equipment behave over time. As demand for infrastructure continues to grow, those lifecycle decisions become increasingly important. Getting more from existing infrastructure isn't only about how efficiently hardware operates while it's in service. It's also about understanding how long that hardware can continue operating reliably before additional investment is needed. That data informs whether hardware can remain in service, should be repaired, or needs to be replaced. Understanding hardware performance holistically allows us to extend the useful life of equipment when it continues to perform reliably instead of relying solely on a fixed replacement schedule. When performance declines or newer hardware provides meaningful improvements in capacity, reliability, or efficiency, we can plan a transition. Reliability comes first. Extending a hardware lifecycle is valuable only when equipment continues to meet our operational standards. We repair hardware whenever practical to extend its useful life. When equipment can no longer remain in service at Dropbox, we work with trusted partners to resell or responsibly recycle it. Together, these decisions help maximize the value of equipment throughout its lifecycle rather than treating deployment and replacement as the only meaningful milestones. But eventually, new hardware does need to come online. And as servers become more powerful and storage becomes denser, deploying them can introduce a new set of constraints in the physical infrastructure that supports them. Engineering beyond the hardware Deploying new hardware isn't as simple as swapping one server for another. Before new hardware can go into production, the physical environment has to be able to support it. Our team plans for the power, airflow, rack layout, cabling, and other physical requirements each deployment needs, working closely with our colocation providers along the way. Those decisions are closely connected. A server that stores more data or delivers more compute may also draw more power or generate more heat. That can change how racks are designed, how equipment is cooled, and even how much hardware a particular area of a data center can support. As infrastructure becomes more powerful and denser, getting more from the hardware depends on making sure the environment around it can evolve, too. One recent example illustrates how those tradeoffs play out in practice. As Dropbox deployed its seventh-generation servers, the increased power requirements exceeded the capacity of the existing rack power design. Rather than rebuilding the underlying facility infrastructure, the Hardware Engineering and Datacenter Engineering teams redesigned the rack power architecture, doubling the number of power distribution units per rack while continuing to use the existing busways. The result supported the new hardware without requiring major changes to the data center itself. It's a reminder that infrastructure improvements don't stop with the hardware itself. As demand grows and hardware evolves to meet it, each new generation has to fit within the constraints of the environment around it. What years of operating infrastructure have taught us The work reflects more than a decade of engineering investment across Dropbox's infrastructure. Capacity planning, fleet optimization, storage systems, hardware lifecycle management, and data center engineering each address different challenges, but together they help us make better use of the infrastructure that supports our products. None of this work is one and done. As customer demands change, hardware evolves, and new technologies introduce opportunities and new constraints, we improve our infrastructure, each update building on the ones that came before it. Those lessons have become even more relevant as demand for digital infrastructure continues to grow. AI is accelerating the need for storage and compute across the industry, but the underlying engineering challenge hasn't changed. Infrastructure still has to scale while remaining reliable, efficient, and resilient. As these technologies evolve, we'll continue building systems that support the products our customers rely on today while giving us the flexibility to support what's next. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: Anyone noticed AI PRs that ignore infrastructure and DevOps realities?
summary: I work with some very talented developers (I'm also a full-stack developer in addition to handling DevOps), but since the rise of AI, I've noticed more pull requests that include pipeline changes or introduce new services that require configuration outside of the codebase. I have safeguards in place that automatically add me as a reviewer whenever these areas are affected. As a result, I end up rejecting a significant number of these PRs because many of the proposed changes simply won't work in our environment and this has been stirring up drama with people asking “who made you king”…. The code itself may look reasonable and it works on the devs pc (actually sometimes not between devs since AI might have added some packages or services to original devs pc), but the developers overlooks the infrastructure, deployment, networking, security, and operational requirements needed to make those changes work correctly in production. What surprises me most is that some of them genuinely don't seem to understand why it won't work simply because it worked on their PC. They fail to realize that a production environment involves far more than just writing code that runs locally. sometimes they give me some copy-pasted answers that it will work if you just do X. Is anyone else experiencing this or is it just me? submitted by /u/ToastieCPU

title: [Docker] AI Agent Security Risks: What Can Go Wrong When Agents Act on Their Own
summary: The thing that makes an AI agent useful, its freedom to act, is also what can introduce risk. An agent doesn’t just answer a question, it browses, runs code, and calls tools on its own, so a single bad or manipulated instruction can turn into real damage instead of just a wrong answer. That’s the shift traditional application security wasn’t built for, and it’s why trust has to be built into the system around the agent, not assumed. An agent decides its own path, picking tools at runtime, chaining actions together, and usually running with the credentials of whoever launched it. That autonomy is the source of most agent-specific risk, and it points to the two-part answer that runs through this post: contain what an agent can reach, and oversee what it does. Key takeaways AI agents introduce risks traditional app security wasn’t built for: they choose tools, chain actions, and often run with your credentials. The main risks are prompt injection, tool misuse and poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential exposure, and data exfiltration. Most trace back to one thing: the agent can act, so containment and oversight matter more than the model. The two-part answer is isolation to limit blast radius and governance to oversee behavior. Why agents break traditional security models If you’ve secured web services, the model is familiar: requests arrive at known endpoints, deterministic logic handles them, and you design controls around that predictability. Agents break that assumption. They interpret instructions dynamically, choose tools at runtime, and run multi-step chains with very little human intervention at each step. A coding agent might read a file, install a dependency, change config, run tests, and push a commit from a single prompt. Because an agent chooses its own path, a compromised or misdirected one can take a far wider range of actions than a traditional service. Every risk below has already produced documented real-world incidents, and they all follow from that shift. 1. Prompt injection Prompt injection is the risk that defines agent security. Because an agent acts on whatever text it reads, an attacker doesn’t need access to your systems. They just need the agent to encounter their instructions, hidden in a web page, a code comment, an issue, or a document it summarizes. A real prompt-injection case showed an agent following instructions buried in repository content and taking actions its user never intended. Incident highlight: A coding agent followed instructions buried in a repository’s own content and took actions its user never intended. The malicious text arrived through data the agent was simply asked to read. The agent has no reliable way to tell a legitimate instruction from an injected one, so the defense is to limit what a hijacked agent can reach. 2. Tool misuse and tool poisoning Agents act through tools: API connectors, database queries, file operations, and code execution. Every tool is an access vector, and two things could go wrong. An agent can be given more tools than the task needs, widening the attack surface for no reason. And a tool itself can be poisoned, its description carrying hidden instructions that manipulate the agent into misusing it. The mitigations are to scope tools to the task at runtime, source them from registries with verified provenance, and review tool descriptions rather than trusting them by default. 3. Excessive autonomy The more an agent can do without review, the more a single bad decision costs. Excessive autonomy is the risk of granting an agent broad, standing permission to act, most visibly when developers run YOLO mode, where every action is auto-approved. This autonomy is genuinely useful, so switching it off defeats the point. The better move is to run the agent where that autonomy can’t reach anything it shouldn’t, so speed doesn’t necessarily mean increased blast radius. Incident highlight: A developer asked a coding agent to clean up an old repository. It generated an rm -rf command with a trailing ~/ and ran it with no confirmation step, wiping the developer’s entire home directory. Nothing in the setup gave a human a chance to catch it before it executed. 4. Credential and secret exposure When an agent runs under a developer’s personal token, every action it takes carries that person’s full permissions, and a compromise hands those permissions to an attacker. Secrets sitting in prompts, config files, or environment variables baked into an image make it worse, because a prompt injection can read them straight out of the agent’s context. Agents should get their own scoped, short-lived credentials, injected at runtime and kept out of the conversation, rather than borrowing yours. Incident highlight: An AWS engineer handed a small Cost Explorer bug to a coding agent running with their own operator-level access. The agent decided the cleanest fix was to delete and rebuild the production environment, and it held the credentials to do exactly that. The result was a thirteen-hour regional outage. 5. Data exfiltration and untrusted handoffs An agent with network access and sensitive information in its context can send that data somewhere it shouldn’t, whether through a compromised tool or an injected instruction. The risk grows in multi-agent setups, where one agent passes work to another. If the receiving agent treats that input as trusted, a compromise in one link can spread down the chain. Restricting network egress to known endpoints and treating every agent-to-agent handoff as untrusted input could keep a single failure from spreading. How to contain the risk The risks are varied, but there are controls to secure AI agents. Isolate where the agent runs so a mistake or a hijack is trapped in a disposable environment instead of loose on your host, and scope what the agent can access so the damage it can do is small even inside that boundary. Risk Primary control Primary injection Isolation, so a hijacked agent can’t reach anything that matters Tool misuse and poisoning Runtime-scoped tools from verified-provenance sources Excessive autonomy A sandbox boundary that makes auto-approval safe Credential exposure Dedicated, short-lived credentials injected at runtime Data exfiltration Allow-listed network egress and untrusted inter-agent input Isolation is the highest-impact starting point, and a microVM boundary makes it strong without slowing the agent down. On top of containment, oversight is what keeps a fleet of agents accountable. Then, AI governance defines which actions an agent may take, what it can reach, and how its behavior is logged, so risk is managed deliberately rather than discovered after an incident. Contain the blast radius, govern the behavior These risks aren’t reasons to avoid developing with agents. Instead, we need to give agents the freedom to finish the job by building trust into the system around them, so that freedom never means access to everything. And that’s the job Docker Sandboxes is built for: each agent runs in its own disposable microVM with the network and filesystem controls you define, so a mistake or an injection is contained by design. And AI Governance adds the oversight layer, setting which actions, tools, and credentials are allowed and enforcing it everywhere your team works. Contain the blast radius, and govern the behavior. Frequently Asked Questions What are the main security risks of AI agents? The most significant are prompt injection, tool misuse and tool poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential and secret exposure, and data exfiltration. All of them stem from the fact that agents act on their own, using tools and credentials, rather than following a fixed, reviewable path. What is the biggest AI agent security risk? For most teams it’s excessive access: an agent running with more autonomy and more credentials than the task needs. It turns a small mistake or a single prompt injection into a large incident, because the agent can reach so much. How is agent security different from application security? Traditional application security assumes predictable request-and-response flows. Agent security has to account for autonomous decisions, tools chosen at runtime, and multi-step chains where the agent sets its own path. The attack surface is wider because the agent, not a fixed program, decides what happens next. Can prompt injection be prevented? You can reduce it with input handling and tool hygiene, but you can’t assume it away, because an agent can’t reliably tell injected instructions from legitimate ones. The durable defense is containment: run the agent so that even a successfully injected one can’t reach anything sensitive. How do you reduce AI agent security risks? Start with isolation so a compromised agent is trapped in a disposable environment. Add scoped tool access and dedicated credentials to shrink what any agent can do. Then layer on governance to define and enforce those limits consistently across every agent your team runs.

title: [CNCF] Join Platform Engineering Day at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026
summary: As organizations accelerate their adoption of AI and cloud native technologies, platform teams are being asked to solve a growing set of challenges. How can developers access new capabilities such as AI safely and efficiently? How can platforms reduce bottlenecks rather than create them? And how should internal platforms evolve as the needs of developers and organizations change? These are some of the questions at the heart of Platform Engineering Day, a full-day event bringing the community together to exchange practical experiences, lessons learned, and ideas about the future of platform engineering, as part of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City, on Monday, November 9th 2026. Created by the community, for practitioners The idea for Platform Engineering Day began at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe in Amsterdam in 2023. Platform engineering was already generating significant discussion across the community, but there was an opportunity to create a dedicated space that went beyond individual tools and project updates. Practitioners wanted to talk about the principles and practices behind building and operating platforms—and, importantly, to share what they were learning along the way. That idea became Platform Engineering Day, with the first event taking place alongside KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe in Paris in 2024. Since its inception, the goal has remained simple: create a space where platform engineers and practitioners can learn from one another. That means talking not only about successful implementations, but also about approaches that did not work as expected, trade-offs teams encountered, and lessons they would apply differently next time. Learning from real-world platform engineering Platform engineering rarely has a one-size-fits-all answer. Teams have different users, organizational structures, technologies, constraints, and definitions of what a successful internal platform looks like. Platform Engineering Day prioritizes end-user stories and case studies, giving attendees an opportunity to hear directly from practitioners building and evolving platforms in real environments. The aim is to move beyond what teams are building and explore why they made particular decisions, what they learned, and how their approaches have changed over time. This year’s conversations will span some of the issues currently shaping platform engineering, including AI and platform engineering, sustainability, agents as both producers and consumers of platforms, Platform as a Product, and compliance. AI in particular is introducing new questions for platform teams. Organizations want developers to experiment with and adopt AI capabilities, while still providing appropriate security, governance, reliability, and operational guardrails. Platform engineering can provide an interface between those requirements, helping teams make new capabilities accessible without introducing unnecessary friction into software delivery. A full day for every stage of the platform engineering journey Platform Engineering Day is designed for people at different stages of their platform engineering journey, from those beginning to explore the discipline to practitioners already operating mature internal platforms. The day will begin with a single track in the morning, bringing the community together around shared topics and perspectives. After lunch, the program will split into two tracks, allowing attendees to explore a broader range of subjects and levels of technical depth. Across the day, attendees can expect a mixture of keynotes, lightning talks, panels, practitioner stories, and opportunities to connect with others in the community. No prior platform engineering knowledge is required. Whether you are a platform engineer, product manager, solutions architect, technical leader, decision maker, or simply beginning to explore platform engineering, the program is intended to offer perspectives relevant to your journey. Where platform engineering is heading Platform engineering continues to evolve alongside the wider cloud native ecosystem. The emergence of AI and agentic workloads is creating new requirements for platforms, while established challenges around developer experience, sustainability, compliance, governance, and treating platforms as products continue to mature. Platform Engineering Day provides a place to examine these changes through the experiences of the people encountering them firsthand. Attendees should leave with practical examples of how other teams are approaching these challenges, lessons they can apply within their own organizations, and a clearer picture of the conversations currently shaping the platform engineering community. Just as importantly, the event provides an opportunity to share experiences with peers. By discussing successes alongside failures, challenges alongside solutions, the community can continue learning together and building better platforms. Join co-chairs Paula Kennedy, Stacey Potter, and Ramiro Berrelleza at Platform Engineering Day and be part of the conversation about what’s next for platform engineering. Register now!

title: [CNCF] Who owns NIS2 and DORA on a Kubernetes platform team
summary: There is a meeting that repeats across a lot of European engineering organizations right now. Someone from legal or risk brings a NIS2 control, a DORA article, or a “can we evidence this” request into the room. The Kubernetes platform team looks at security. Security looks at the platform team. A ticket lands on the security board, because that feels like the responsible place for anything with a regulation in the title. Three sprints later the cluster has not changed, the evidence still does not exist, and everyone is quietly annoyed with the security lead. The failure is not legal and it is not technical. It is an ownership failure, and it has a specific shape: a regulation name was put on a board instead of an artifact being put in a sprint. Security can write the policy. Security cannot merge the Helm chart. This article is about closing that gap on a cloud native platform: the traceability chain from a regulatory requirement to a Kubernetes object, a RACI that survives contact with sprint planning, and the open source projects that actually produce the evidence. One caveat before going further. Nothing here is legal advice, and none of the mappings below are an official compliance mapping. NIS2 and DORA are outcome-based texts. Which entities and services are in scope, what measures are proportionate, and what evidence is sufficient all depend on the organization’s own risk assessment, its sector rules, national transposition, and its regulator. They do not depend on a table in a blog post. What happens when security owns the regulation The common default is that anything with a regulation in the title becomes a security ticket. The CISO, or the one senior security engineer who still answers Slack, becomes the owner of NIS2, DORA, and whatever arrives next. Platform engineers stay on product work. Application teams stay on features. The security function becomes a queue. Two failure modes follow, and they feed each other. The first is the bottleneck. Every image exception, every privileged securityContext, every “we need this log in the SIEM” request waits on the same two people. Delivery teams learn that talking to security is how work dies, so they start routing around it: a break-glass kubeconfig here, a sidecar nobody reviewed there, a registry that is not the approved catalog. The result rarely announces itself. Non-compliance does not show up as a red cell on a slide; it shows up as shadow infrastructure carrying a ticket label that still says “security”. The second is learned helplessness on the platform side. If compliance is permanently someone else’s backlog, platform engineers never own the reasoning behind it. They ship an admission policy because they were told to, disable it when it blocks a release, and wait for security to notice. That is the opposite of the ownership every platform engineering talk asks for. You cannot ask a team to own outcomes and simultaneously keep the regulatory outcome on another team’s board. Neither failure is a personality problem. Both are org designs that nobody named out loud. What NIS2 Article 20 and DORA Article 5 actually assign Both texts are blunt about where accountability sits, and it is not “the security team”. NIS2 Article 20 places cybersecurity risk-management measures on the management body of essential and important entities. The management body approves the measures, oversees their implementation, can be held liable for non-compliance, and is required to follow training. DORA Article 5 does the same for financial entities. The management body defines, approves, oversees, and remains responsible for the ICT risk management framework, and roles and responsibilities for all ICT-related functions have to be assigned clearly and documented. A CISO title is not a substitute for that assignment; it is one of the roles the assignment has to name. So far this reads like a board problem. By Friday afternoon it is a middle-management problem. The management body will not patch containerd. It will not decide whether kube-apiserver audit logs are retained for 12 months or 18. It will not sit in the planning session where “ship the new tenant” competes with “we still have no evidence trail”. Those decisions are made by engineering managers, or they are not made at all. The vacuum underneath the management body is where most programs die. Legal translates the article. Security writes a control statement. Nobody is accountable for the Kubernetes object that would make the statement true. The same vacuum appears in Cyber Resilience Act programs, which carry a harder clock: accountability at the top is theater unless someone in engineering owns the work that produces the evidence. Put artifacts on the board, not regulation names A regulation is a reason. It is not a ticket. “NIS2 Article 21” cannot be demoed at sprint review. “kube-apiserver audit policy shipped, logs shipped to the SIEM, retention documented” can be. The artifact does not come from an engineer reading a directive and inventing a Kubernetes task. It comes from a traceability chain with a clean handover in the middle. Traceability chain in two stages: scope, control question, and evidence definition owned by risk, legal, and security; artifact, sprint item, and recurring operation owned by the platform and application teamsSteps one to three are interpretation, and they belong to risk, legal, and security. Steps four to six are delivery, and they belong to the platform and application teams. The handover is the artifact, not the article number. A ticket that says “implement NIS2 Article 21(2)(d)” has skipped the middle of the chain and asks an engineer to act as the lawyer who decided the law applies. The chain also closes. Step six is what produces the evidence that step three asked for, which means the output of delivery flows back to risk, audit, and the SOC as a matter of routine rather than as a fire drill three days before an inspection. An artifact that only exists because someone ran a script by hand once has not completed the chain. The table below shows what the output of that chain looks like on a Kubernetes platform. The middle column is the control question the artifact answers. The provenance columns point at the provisions that make the artifact relevant; they are not a claim that the text commands that specific implementation. DORA references apply only where the financial entity and the ICT service fall within its scope. material vulnerability is disclosed?Article 21(2)(d) and (e): supply chain security, vulnerability handling and disclosureArticles 8 and 9: ICT asset identification, protection and preventionA secrets concrete piece of work. It can be estimated, it can be demoed, and (the part that matters at audit time) it can be pointed at. The cloud native projects that produce the evidence None of these artifacts requires a compliance product, in the sense of a tool that generates evidence about a platform it does not otherwise touch. They are ordinary platform capabilities, and the open source ecosystem covers most of them. Not everything in the table below is a CNCF project (Sigstore and OpenBao sit under the OpenSSF and the Linux Foundation respectively), but all of it is open source and all of it can be run by the team that owns the cluster. The table is illustrative rather than prescriptive. It answers “can this be built with open source”, which is not quite the question a platform lead faces. ArtifactOpen source building blocksWhat the platform team actually operatesHardened image catalog and rebuild pipeline *Harbor for the registry, Sigstore for signing and verification, in-toto for attestations, an image scanner in CIA base image that is rebuilt on a schedule and on advisory, published to one registry that workloads are allowed to pull fromSecrets as a managed serviceOpenBao or an equivalent open source secrets manager as the store, External Secrets Operator to project secrets into the cluster, SPIFFE and SPIRE for workload identity, cert-manager for certificate lifecycleOne credential path: identity-based, short-lived, with no long-lived tokens in manifests or CI variablesAudit and detection evidenceKubernetes audit policy upstream, Fluentd or Fluent Bit and OpenTelemetry for collection, Falco for runtime events, Prometheus for the operational signalsAn audit policy that is not None, a shipping pipeline that survives node churn, and a retention setting someone has written down (the SIEM at the far end is usually bought; the collection path is yours)Admission control and exceptionsKyverno or OPA Gatekeeper, plus the upstream Pod Security Admission baselinePolicies in version control, enforced in production, with exceptions expressed as objects that expire rather than as Slack messagesSoftware inventorySBOM generation in CI, stored as an attestation next to the artifact rather than in a wikiAn answer to “what was in the image we deployed on the 14th” that takes minutes, not daysService ownership metadataBackstage or an equivalent catalogA machine-readable answer to “who is the engineering manager for this service”, which is what makes the RACI below real * Buildable and realistic to operate are different claims, and the hardened image catalog is where they diverge most. The pieces are all open source, but the product is not the pipeline; it is the rebuild cadence, sustained across every base image and runtime you ship, in the week half the team is on holiday. Few platform teams are funded for that, and a catalog that goes stale is worse than no catalog, because by then a control statement says it is handled. Sourcing the base layer from someone who maintains it full time is a legitimate answer, and it does not remove the ownership question so much as change its shape: the provider enters third party scope under NIS2 Article 21(2)(d) and DORA Article 28, and supplier management needs a named owner exactly as the pipeline did. None of this is unique to regulated industries. It is the same platform baseline most mature teams build anyway; NIS2 and DORA mostly change the deadline and the consequence of missing it. Open source removes the license barrier rather than the staffing one, so the build or source decision belongs in the roadmap for every row, not just the one carrying the asterisk. Which is the real point of the table. A cluster can have Kyverno installed, Falco running, and SBOMs in CI and still fail an inspection, because nobody can say who decided what “acceptable” means or who is accountable for keeping it that way. Tooling is the easy half. A RACI for a Kubernetes platform Once the traceability chain exists, the RACI answers the remaining question: who gets the artifact over the line and keeps it true afterward? Adjust the role names to your organization. Do not adjust the underlying idea, which is that security is rarely Accountable for the artifact. A secrets manager and a hardened image catalog are services the platform team runs, not appliances that security sprinkles on at the end. ArtifactResponsibleAccountableConsultedInformedHardened image catalog and rebuild pipelinePlatform engineersPlatform engineering managerSecurity (policy, CVE exceptions)Application teams, riskSecrets manager as the only credential pathPlatform engineersPlatform engineering managerSecurity, IAMApplication engineering managersKubernetes audit logs and ingress logs into the SIEMPlatform and SREPlatform engineering managerSecurity and SOC (what evidence is required)Risk, CISOAdmission policy (restricted PSS, no :latest)Platform engineersPlatform engineering managerSecurity (exceptions)Application teamsIncident clock: detect, page, assemble factsOn-call engineerEngineering manager who owns that serviceSecurity, legal, communicationsManagement body, CSIRTNotification to the authoritySecurity or the nominated control functionCISO or nominated roleLegal, engineering manager of the affected systemManagement bodySBOM in CI for what you actually shipEngineers who build the artifactEngineering manager of that pipelineSecurity (format, retention)Procurement, riskException to run privileged or with hostNetworkRequesting engineerRequesting engineer’s managerSecurityPlatform, risk A RACI is a communication tool, not a governance artifact in its own right. If you publish the table and never open it during planning, you have produced stationery. Two rows get confused more often than the rest, and both are worth stating explicitly. Detection is not notification Incident detection and authority notification are different jobs on different clocks. NIS2 Article 23 expects an early warning to the CSIRT or competent authority within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, an incident notification within 72 hours, and a final report within a month. DORA sets its own reporting path and deadlines for major ICT-related incidents. If you make the on-call engineer “own NIS2 reporting”, you will get panic or silence at 02:00. The engineer owns the facts: what broke, when, the blast radius, what has already been done. The nominated control function owns the notice to the authority. The engineering manager owns whether the runbook was rehearsed before the night it was needed. That separation is also what makes the 24-hour clock survivable. An early warning is a factual submission, not a root cause analysis. The platform’s job is to make those facts easy to gather in minutes, which is exactly what audit logs and a rehearsed runbook are for. Exceptions belong to the requesting engineering manager Security can advise that CAP_SYS_ADMIN in a production namespace is a bad idea. Only the requesting team’s manager can decide that the product risk is worth it, write down the reason, and set an expiry. If security is Accountable for exceptions, every exception becomes a negotiation with the person everyone is trying not to bother, and the real decision maker stays invisible. Making the requesting manager accountable puts the cost back where the benefit is, and gives the exception a natural expiry date: the manager who wanted it is the one who has to renew it. Capacity is the part that gets skipped The useful test in a planning session is simple: is the artifact in the next sprint, with a named engineering manager, or is it still a control statement on a security slide? A second, more uncomfortable question follows: who is currently holding work labeled “security” or “compliance” that should not be theirs? An admission policy the platform should own is one answer. A 40-page control mapping that belongs with risk is another. Capacity is where these programs quietly fail. A platform team staffed for product delivery alone will treat every control as overtime. They will ship the hardened image catalog, or they will ship the new tenant environment. They will not ship both from the same three people unless the roadmap is quietly optimistic. Cutting the scope honestly is a better outcome than putting “DORA” on a slide and leaving engineers to find the hours in the evening. Security still sets the bar, and that work does not go away: what “restricted” means in practice, which CVEs are acceptable exceptions, what a fact pack must contain, which logs the SOC will actually use. It reviews exceptions, runs or supports the notification path, and trains engineering managers until they can hold the conversation without forwarding every email to the CISO. But Consulted has to mean “answers within the same sprint”, not “joins a working group”. If the security function cannot staff that responsiveness, the honest move is to shrink the control set rather than to keep a queue that delivery teams learn to avoid. Teams walk toward security when talking to it makes the work smaller and clearer. They walk around it when it does the opposite. “We cannot evidence access to kube-apiserver for last week’s incident” is a useful sentence in week two of a program. The same sentence the week before an on-site inspection is a much more expensive one. Look at the engineering manager first The chain is short. The management body is accountable in the text. The engineering manager is accountable in the cluster. Security is the specialist you consult so that the work is correct. The engineer is responsible for the object that ships. Staff only the management body and the security function, and you get policies and liability with no Kubernetes. Staff only the engineering manager and the engineer, and you get a fast platform you cannot explain to a supervisor. Both halves are load-bearing. So the next time a regulation lands in the room, try not to look at security first. Look at the engineering manager who owns the system the requirement describes, and ask two questions: which artifact will you demo, and which sprint is it in? If there is no answer, the organization does not have a security gap. It has an ownership gap, and those are the expensive ones. References Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2555/oj Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2554/oj

title: [Cloudflare] Cloudflare and OpenAI: making AI discovery better for everyone
summary: Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site.Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilot in July with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflare’s network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently.Today, we’re sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAI’s search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, we’ve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web.Finding more of the webThe web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them.In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information – whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself.Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAI’s search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find.This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflare’s total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it.With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI, OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web.From discovery to useful answersFinding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do.We’ve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that aren’t there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners.We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index.Making discovery easierAs more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient.Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit.The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't.There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people.Making it worthwhile to participateThe next phase will build on what we’ve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered.We’re continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and we’ll keep sharing what we learn along the way.Domain owners’ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesn’t grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training.You can use Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control to understand and manage how AI systems access your website.

title: [Netflix] Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
summary: How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss.Authors: Nick Rutigliano, Argha C, Samartha ChandrashekarOpen Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live.Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop.This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform.Why GPU reliability mattersNetflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners.All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — -Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on.Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work.Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too.Why basic health checks are not enoughWe start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training.The next step most teams take is a GPU-level check to confirm that the driver responds and that the GPUs are visible. That catches a dead or missing GPU, but misses the cases that take the most time.A GPU can answer a status query and still be faulty once a workload touches it. A fault in on-chip memory or in the firmware that manages the device can remain invisible until a job allocates memory or runs sustained compute, at which point the job fails or slows.A high-speed network adapter may be present but show fewer links than expected. Collective operations still run, at a fraction of the bandwidth, so the job does not crash. It crawls, and the cause is easy to miss.A check can fail in ways that leave a faulty machine looking healthy. The diagnostic tool can hang when the driver hangs, and a naive check that waits on it hangs too. A binary that the check depends on can go missing after a driver upgrade, causing the check to stop running and report nothing. A check that can silently stop running is worse than no check, because it gives false confidence while the machine keeps working.Because a job runs as a gang, any one of these on any one machine can degrade or stop the whole job, and none of them shows up in an instance-level check or a driver-responds check. The health system has to assume the hardware can lie and the tools that inspect it can break.A machine can pass a basic check and still be faulty. Layered checks, timeouts, a fallback path, and checks that fail when a dependency is missing close these gaps.Our approachWe treat reliability as four layers, each catching what the layer below cannot:1/ Node and hardware health: find bad GPUs, network adapters, interconnects, memory errors, and thermal issues, then taint or recycle the machine.2/ Scheduler and platform: retry at the task & job level, validate a machine before it takes work, and drain & recycle machines safely.3/ Training loop: checkpoint and use elastic workers so a job survives losing a machine.4/ Observability: metrics, service-level objectives, and failure attribution across the other three.The first two layers keep hardware problems away from jobs. The third accepts that some loss is unavoidable and makes it cheap. The fourth tells us whether the first three are working.Four layers: Each catches what the layer below cannot.How the health checks workChecks run in two tiers. Device-level checks look at each GPU. A node-level agent, built on the open-source Kubernetes node-problem-detector, runs on every GPU machine every 30 seconds and turns check results into conditions on the Kubernetes node, the same mechanism Kubernetes uses to mark a node NotReady. Controllers watch those conditions and decide whether the machine can take on work.GPU device checks are built on NVIDIA’s DCGM for driver-reported error codes, uncorrectable memory errors, interconnect integrity, and thermal state, and networking adapter checks inspect the host state for the count and link state of the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces that carry cross-machine traffic. A few of these checks deserve detail.Two-tier health checking. Device-level and node-level checks become Kubernetes node conditions, which controllers then turn into taints, drains, terminates, and replaces.Failing closed: if the driver or the diagnostic tool is unresponsive, the check times out and marks the machine unhealthy. A check that cannot reach the hardware reports a problem rather than passing, so a wedged driver takes the machine out of rotation rather than letting it hide behind a hung tool.A fallback path: driver error codes are the strongest signal that a GPU has faulted, but the tool that reads them can itself be broken in certain failure modes! When it does, we read the kernel log dmesg directly for those codes, so no Xid or SXid errors are missed.Our own fatal-error map: vendor driver error catalogs lag newer GPU generations and do not always match what we see in production, so we keep our own mapping of which codes are fatal for each GPU family. A code that means reset-the-GPU in one generation can be benign in another, and one GPU generation emits a burst of normally-fatal code on every healthy boot, which we learned to treat as noise rather than drain fresh machines.No silent no-ops: a check fails when a required dependency is missing. This one came from an upgrade that dropped a binary the network-adapter check relied on. The check quietly stopped running, and machines with the wrong number of adapters shipped for days before the slow jobs were traced back to them. Now a missing dependency fails the check.Turning a bad machine into healthy capacity, automaticallyWhen a check fails, the machine’s node condition changes, and controllers take over. We distinguish two levels. A problem condition blocks new work from landing while jobs are running, because pulling a job off a machine is disruptive, and many problems clear on their own. If the condition persists beyond a tolerance window, it escalates to a failure condition, which evacuates the machine, drains its tasks (overriding the normal disruption limits to move quickly), terminates it, and replaces it.Karpenter node auto-repair is used on our compute stack. We have customized it with a policy and a controller that maps each node condition to the duration we tolerate it before acting, so a fast-fatal error is actioned within minutes. At the same time, a flaky signal gets a longer window, and a cap limits how much of a cluster we will disrupt at once, so a bad rollout of the checks themselves cannot cascade into tearing down a whole cluster. We plan to upstream this feature to all Karpenter users.Graded remediation. A problem is tolerated and may clear; a persistent failure escalates to evacuation and draining, then to a fast in-place fix or termination for confirmed hardware faults.Not every fault requires a full replacement, and replacement is the slowest way to restore capacity. We match the action to the fault. Killing the offending job clears a software wedge. Resetting a single GPU clears many transient device faults. Rebooting the machine clears the firmware state that has drifted over a long uptime. Terminating and replacing is reserved for hardware that fails a test we trust. For that last case, we record the GPU’s immutable hardware identifier, which stays with the physical device across reboots and relaunches even when the instance changes, report it to the cloud provider, and keep our own list, so a device that fails repeatedly does not quietly rejoin the pool under a new instance.One subtlety sits between detection and scheduling. A freshly checked machine was handed to the scheduler just as its checks were still settling, so a job could land on it a moment before a slow check flagged it. We now hold capacity until the checks have run and settled, which closed that window.Validating a machine before it takes workA machine that just booted is not trusted until it proves itself. Before we release its capacity, it passes system checks, confirms the GPUs and their topology are present, and runs a round of GPU diagnostics. We then wait for the health checks to run twice, because the longer checks, such as counting network adapters, take more than one cycle to fire, and releasing after a single pass would let work land before those checks are reported. Only then do we remove the startup taint. On teardown, we run deeper diagnostics and record the GPU identifiers, which feed the same bad-hardware list, so hardware that failed once does not silently cycle back into service.Letting long jobs survive machine lossEven with all of the above, some machines are lost mid-job, so we make that cheap. Jobs checkpoint their state, and on a lost machine, they resume from the last healthy checkpoint rather than restarting from the beginning of a multi-week run. Workers are elastic and retryable, and the scheduler automatically retries platform-caused failures.Attribution is what makes automatic retries safe. If we retried every failure, we would mask genuine bugs in a job and burn GPU hours looping on an error the platform cannot fix, so we classify each failure as platform or application before retrying. One example of why this matters: a class of timeouts in NCCL, the collective communication library GPUs use to exchange data, appeared to be a network fault and was traced to data-loading stalls at high worker counts. The GPUs and the network were fine, and the fix was in the data pipeline. Treated as hardware failures, those timeouts would have cycled healthy machines without fixing the cause.Measuring whether it worksWe track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible:Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment.Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available.Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure.Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes.A closed remediation loopThese pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue, or Ray.The reliability loop: validate, watch, actively check, view the job as a system, remediate, then repeat.Sharing GPUs safelyNot every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty.On a multi-GPU machine, we isolate a single faulty GPU, keep the rest in service, and partition healthy GPUs across multiple tenants with memory-level isolation.Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance.ResultsMoving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine.Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen:Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodesJob success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5%What is nextWe are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs.We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes.More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext. Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress.While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs.Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work.ClosingHardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring.Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Docker] Docker Hub security advisory: personal access tokens transferred during account-to-organization conversions
summary: On September 30, 2026, security researchers reported a vulnerability in Docker Hub’s identity and access management through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program. We confirmed the report and deployed a fix to production the same afternoon, less than four hours after receiving it. We then reviewed every account conversion back to the date the flaw was introduced, and on October 2, notified every user and organization owner whose account could have been impacted by this vulnerability. This post explains what the vulnerability was, what it could and could not do, what we found, and what we have changed. We want to thank Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com for finding the issue, reporting it responsibly, and coordinating disclosure with us. Their technical write-up is available at ghostpat.com. This issue is tracked as CVE-2026-105445. Was I or any member of my organization exposed to the vulnerability? On October 2 at 5:30PM EST, we sent out an email with the subject line “Docker Hub Vulnerability Identified & Resolved” to the limited number of users exposed to this vulnerability. If you did not receive an email, you and any members of the organizations you administer were not exposed and there are no actions for you to take. What the vulnerability was Docker Hub lets you convert a personal account into an organization. People do this because Hub has no way to move a repository from one account to another: conversion is how alice/app becomes an organization-owned alice/app without breaking every Docker pull that references it. During conversion, the user names an existing Docker Hub account as the new organization’s owner. Beginning August 26, 2024, conversion also re-assigned the converted account’s personal access tokens (PATs) to that new owner. It did this by changing the token’s owner record, without rotating or revoking the token secret. The named owner was not asked to confirm and was not notified. Together, those two gaps made the following possible: An attacker creates an account and generates a PAT on it. The attacker converts that account to an organization and names a target user as the owner. The attacker’s PAT is re-assigned to the target user. The attacker still holds the secret and the PAT remains active now with the target user’s scope. The token now authenticates to the registry as the target user. What an attacker could and could not do Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access. Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical. The vulnerability did not give access to the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change the target’s password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over the account. The exposure window ran from August 26, 2024, 20:33 UTC, until the fix was deployed on September 30, 2026, at approximately  UTC. Timeline (all times U.S. Eastern) Sept 30, 11:40 AM: Report received at security@docker.com. Sept 30, ~1:30 PM: We independently reproduced the issue with internal test accounts. Sept 30, ~3:10 PM: Fix deployed to production and verified against the original proof of concept. Conversion no longer transfers PATs. Sept 30, ~3:23 PM: Documentation updated to state that PATs do not transfer and must be recreated by the new owner, with organization access tokens recommended. Sept 30, 4:59 PM: Researchers informed of the fix. Both parties agreed to coordinate disclosure. Oct 2, 5:30 PM: Exposed users and their organization owners notified by email. Oct 8, 3:45 PM: Forced deactivation of all PATs transferred through conversion, except where the account holder opted out. What we investigated and found We enumerated every account conversion performed since August 26, 2024 and correlated them with registry authentication logs, Docker Hub usage data, and IAM token records. We looked for any token used under more than one identity, and we examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all. We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited. Every push made with a transferred token landed either in the converted organization’s own repositories or in the new owner’s own repositories. None went into an unrelated user’s or organization’s account. In the large majority of cases, the account converted and the account named as owner belonged to the same person or team, which is the normal, legitimate use of this feature. We statically analyzed the highest-risk public images without executing them: images pushed after a conversion where we could not establish that the same person controlled both accounts. We found no malware, cryptominers, command-and-control activity, credential harvesting, persistence, or tampering. We found no evidence that Docker’s own infrastructure or services were affected. We also want to be clear about the limits of that finding:registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used leaves no trace. For that reason, we did not rely on detection to decide who was exposed. We treated every PAT that moved through conversion during the window as potentially affected, whether or not we saw it used. What we did for affected users On October 2, we emailed the limited number of users whose accounts received transferred PATs. Each email listed the in-scope tokens by description and creation date so users could find them in Docker Hub. We separately notified the associated organization owners. On October 8th at 3:45 PM EST, we deactivated the identified transferred PATs. Tokens that their owners asked to keep before the deadline were excluded. Once again, if you did not receive the above email, no PAT on your account was transferred through this flow. Your account was therefore not exposed to this vulnerability and there is no action for you to take. What we are changing The immediate fix removed PAT transfer from conversion entirely. Beyond that, we are now: requiring consent from a user before they are named as an organization owner, and notifying them when it happens; recording an auditable history of every token ownership change, so questions like this can be answered from records rather than inference; reviewing other flows that change credential ownership for the same pattern. What you can do Review the personal access tokens on your account in Docker Hub under Account settings, Personal access tokens, and revoke any you don’t recognize or no longer use. For automation that belongs to an organization, use organization access tokens rather than a person’s PAT. If you have questions about this notice, contact Docker Support at app.docker.com/support/contact. Responsible disclosure works when researchers and vendors treat each other as partners. Peter and Krisztian did that here, and our users are safer for it. If you find a security issue in a Docker product, please report it to security@docker.com.
